answer.rationale: The primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, and the line is running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer — any supply interruption or onboarding hiccup would directly threaten delivery, which the objective treats as a hard constraint, not a tradeable variable. That rules out switching vendors (memory_c2) or adding a second source this cycle: both require qualification/onboarding lead time we don't have, and memory_c3's second-source success doesn't establish it can be stood up in 14 days under volume pressure. Negotiate_terms is foreclosed by the situation itself — the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, so memory_c4 (renegotiation recovering margin) is contradicted by current facts and shouldn't be acted on. Defer_decision isn't viable either since this is the primary, non-optional contract (unlike the non-critical case in memory_c5) and it lapses without action. That leaves renewing the incumbent (memory_c1: stable integration, no interruption) as the only option compatible with zero delivery risk. However, straight renewal doesn't touch the 18% cost mandate. Memory_c6 suggests multi-year commitment with the same incumbent can cut unit cost via volume pricing without narrowing scope, which is a different lever than reopening this cycle's price — but I want to verify that record before treating it as a live option, since it's old enough (day 65) that terms or incumbent posture may have shifted, and I don't want to over-apply it given the incumbent's current refusal stance. I'm sizing this as a small_guarded_test rather than locking a full multi-year term immediately: pursue a shorter renewal or a capped multi-year trial with the incumbent while flagging to finance that the 18% target is not fully met this cycle, and revisit cost reduction via second-sourcing or a fuller renegotiation next review once there's lead time to do it without risking delivery.
